claim: Genome-wide TSS usage maps were generated by RAMPAGE assays for developmental series in five Drosophila species spanning 25-50 million years of evolution.
source: Genome-wide TSS usage maps were generated by RAMPAGE assays for developmental series in five species. These datasets constitute single-nucleotide measurements of transcriptional activity at 1 hr resolution throughout embryonic development, and a global survey of its evolution over 25-50MY.
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental approach (RAMPAGE) and the phylogenetic span of the study. Figure 1A shows the experimental design across five species.

claim: RAMPAGE provides single-nucleotide measurements of transcriptional activity at 1 hr resolution throughout embryonic development.
source: These datasets constitute single-nucleotide measurements of transcriptional activity at 1 hr resolution throughout embryonic development, and a global survey of its evolution over 25-50MY.
evidence: The text explicitly states the temporal and spatial resolution of the RAMPAGE method.

claim: For each species, 2.2 × 10^4 to 2.7 × 10^4 high-confidence TSCs were identified.
source: For each species, we identified 2.2 × 104 to 2.7 × 104 high-confidence TSCs.
evidence: Direct statement of the number of TSCs identified per species from the data analysis.

claim: 82% of D. melanogaster TSCs can be attributed to annotated genes.
source: We can thus attribute 82% of D. melanogaster TSCs to annotated genes, the remaining 18% potentially driving the expression of unannotated non-protein-coding transcripts.
evidence: Direct quantification of TSC attribution to annotated genes based on data analysis.

claim: The quantification of promoter expression levels is highly reproducible across biological replicates with Pearson R2 = 0.95 for TSCs with maximum expression ≥25 RPM.
source: Indeed, this analysis shows excellent reproducibility (Pearson R2 = 0.95) for TSCs with maximum expression ≥25 reads per million (RPM, Figure 2A and Figure 2—figure supplement 1), and very good reproducibility (Pearson R2 = 0.92) with maximum expression ≥10 RPM (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Statistical analysis of biological replicates shown in Figure 1D-E and quantified in the text.

claim: The expression profiles of individual promoters are overall tightly conserved across species.
source: For all genes with one-to-one orthologs, the expression profiles are overall tightly conserved across species (Figure 2C), but with substantial gene-to-gene variability (Figure 2—figure supplement 4)
evidence: Analysis of orthologous genes across species shown in Figure 2C demonstrates conservation patterns.

claim: The degree of expression divergence differs substantially between Gene Ontology annotation categories.
source: We found a strong relationship between selective constraints on expression specificity and gene function: indeed, the degree of expression divergence differs substantially between Gene Ontology (GO) annotation categories (Figure 2D).
evidence: Statistical analysis (p<10^-16, one-way ANOVA) of expression divergence by GO category shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Functions related to the regulation of transcription and splicing display the strongest conservation of expression.
source: Functions related to the regulation of transcription and splicing display the strongest conservation of expression, in accordance with the known molecular function of many master regulators of early development.
evidence: Analysis of GO categories shows differential conservation patterns, with transcription/splicing regulation showing highest conservation.

claim: Three major classes of core promoters are defined by distinct sets of core motifs and are associated with three broad phases of embryonic development.
source: We report that distinct types of core promoters are selectively active in three broad phases of embryonic development: specific combinations of core motifs mediate transcription during Early, Intermediate and Late embryogenesis.
evidence: The abstract and results section describe the identification of three promoter classes with distinct temporal activities.

claim: The Early expression class is enriched for DRE and Ohler-1/5/6/7 motifs and consists of promoters for maternally deposited transcripts.
source: The Early expression class, enriched for DRE and Ohler-1/5/6/7 motifs, consists of the promoters for maternally deposited transcripts, including the housekeeping cluster.
evidence: Analysis of core promoter motif enrichment in expression clusters shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Intermediate class is enriched for Initiator (INR), MTE and DPE motifs and mediates transcription throughout mid-embryogenesis.
source: The Intermediate class, enriched for Initiator (INR), MTE and DPE motifs, mediates transcription throughout a broad phase of mid-embryogenesis, from the onset of zygotic expression to the end of organogenesis.
evidence: Analysis of core promoter motif enrichment in expression clusters shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The Late class is enriched for TATA boxes and drives transcription around the transition to the first larval stage.
source: The Late class, enriched for TATA boxes, drives transcription around the transition to the first larval stage.
evidence: Analysis of core promoter motif enrichment in expression clusters shown in Figure 3B.

claim: A classifier trained on core motif scores can predict the three promoter classes with substantial predictive power.
source: In addition, we were able to train a classifier with substantial predictive power to distinguish the three promoter classes based solely on core motif scores (Figure 3D).
evidence: Quadratic discriminant analysis results shown in Figure 3D demonstrate predictive capability.

claim: Different sets of TFBSs are enriched near the core promoters active in the three developmental phases.
source: Sequences proximal to the three core promoter classes are also enriched for different sets of TFBSs (Figure 3E).
evidence: TFBS enrichment analysis shown in Figure 3E identifies distinct binding site preferences for each promoter class.

claim: The presence of most core promoter motifs and TFBSs is conserved between species far beyond random expectations.
source: The presence of most core promoter motifs and TFBSs is conserved between species far beyond random expectations (Figure 3F), which validates the overall quality of our motif predictions.
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 3F with FDR-corrected chi-square tests demonstrates significant conservation.

claim: The three promoter classes display markedly different profiles of sequence conservation.
source: We found that the three promoter classes display markedly different profiles of sequence conservation (Figure 3H and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: PhastCons sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 3H reveals distinct conservation patterns.

claim: There is a subtle but highly significant correlation between the conservation of promoter sequence and that of expression profiles.
source: To further explore the selective pressures acting on regulatory sequences, we investigated quantitative relationships between the evolution of promoter structure (primary sequence) and function (expression specificity). We report a subtle but highly significant correlation between the conservation of promoter sequence and that of expression profiles (Figure 4A–B).
evidence: Correlation analysis shown in Figure 4A-B with statistical significance (p-values provided).

claim: Promoters with highly divergent expression profiles are depleted of sites under purifying selection and enriched for sites under positive selection.
source: Promoters with highly divergent expression profiles are depleted of sites under purifying selection, and enriched for sites under positive selection (Figure 4C–D).
evidence: PhyloP analysis shown in Figure 4C-D quantifies sites under different selection regimes.

claim: Promoters with highly conserved expression profiles tend to have core promoter elements whose sequence is closer to the motif consensus.
source: We found that promoters with highly conserved expression profiles tend to have core promoter elements whose sequence is closer to the motif consensus (Figure 4F), and those in turn tend to be more conserved at the sequence level (Figure 4G).
evidence: Analysis of motif strength versus expression conservation shown in Figure 4F-G.

claim: Only 49% of D. melanogaster TSCs are functionally conserved in all five species.
source: And indeed, we observed widespread birth and death of promoters throughout the clade: only 49% of D. melanogaster TSCs are functionally conserved in all five species (Figure 5A).
evidence: Functional conservation analysis shown in Figure 5A quantifies TSC conservation across species.

claim: When restricted to TSCs with syntenic alignments to other genomes, the functional conservation rate is 75%.
source: To rule out genome assembly artifacts, we restricted our analysis to those with syntenic alignments to other genomes, and measured a functional conservation rate of 75% (Figure 5A).
evidence: Conservation analysis controlling for alignment quality shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The false positive rate for gain/loss event detection is under 0.1%.
source: The analysis of replicates for the D. melanogaster time series shows the false positive rate for gain/loss event detection to be under 0.1% (Figure 5A).
evidence: Replicate analysis shown in Figure 5A provides estimate of false positive rate.

claim: The species phylogeny can be accurately reconstructed from patterns of TSC gain and loss.
source: Consistent with this, we can reconstruct the known species phylogeny by treating the presence or absence of individual TSCs as binary discrete characters in a standard parsimony framework (Figure 5B).
evidence: Phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 5B demonstrates that TSC presence/absence patterns reflect evolutionary relationships.

claim: Promoters active in all species display far higher sequence conservation than species-specific ones.
source: Functional conservation is reflected in sequence conservation: promoters active in all species display far higher sequence conservation than species-specific ones, which appear no more constrained than surrounding regions (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: PhastCons analysis shown in Figure 5C compares sequence conservation between conserved and species-specific promoters.

claim: Non-genic promoters evolve at a substantially higher rate than genic ones.
source: We found a stark contrast in the degree of functional conservation of the two classes, with novel non-genic promoters evolving at a substantially higher rate than genic ones (Figure 5D).
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 5D demonstrates differential conservation rates (p<0.01 for all pairwise comparisons).

claim: 3973 embryonic TSCs in D. melanogaster represent putative lncRNA promoters.
source: We found 3682 embryonic TSCs in D. melanogaster that could not be functionally linked to any annotated protein-coding or small RNA gene, and could therefore represent putative lncRNA promoters. We also identified TSCs for 291 annotated lncRNAs, bringing the total up to 3973.
evidence: Identification of TSCs not associated with protein-coding genes from the data analysis.

claim: Putative lncRNA TSCs correspond to genuine promoters as confirmed by DNaseI hypersensitivity data.
source: The analysis of published genome-wide DNaseI hypersensitivity data (Thomas et al., 2011) confirmed that these putative lncRNA TSCs are likely to correspond to genuine promoters (Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Integration with published DNase-seq data shown in Figure 6B validates promoter activity.

claim: The vast majority of putative lncRNA transcripts do not overlap annotated protein-coding sequences.
source: Most of them appear to correspond to full-length transcripts, and the vast majority of putative lncRNAs do not overlap annotated protein-coding sequences (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Transcript model analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2 demonstrates independence from coding sequences.

claim: The overwhelming majority of candidate lncRNA transcripts are unlikely to encode proteins or peptides as short as 10 amino acids.
source: Analyses of protein-coding potential confirm that the overwhelming majority of transcripts are unlikely to encode proteins, or even peptides as short as 10 amino acids (Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: PhyloCSF analysis shown in Figure 6C quantifies protein-coding potential.

claim: lncRNA promoters tend to be substantially more stage-specific than protein-coding gene promoters as measured by Shannon entropy.
source: As a class, they tend to be substantially more stage-specific than their protein-coding gene counterparts, as measured by the Shannon entropy of their activity profiles (Figure 6D).
evidence: Shannon entropy analysis shown in Figure 6D demonstrates higher temporal specificity of lncRNA promoters.

claim: 631 lncRNA TSCs are active in all five species and display sequence conservation similar to protein-coding gene promoters.
source: In order to investigate whether lncRNA promoters are under purifying selection, we focused on an extremely stringently selected set of 631 TSCs that are active in all five species. This set includes well-known essential noncoding transcription units, such as bithoraxoid (Lipshitz et al., 1987; Petruk et al., 2006) (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and roX1 (Franke and Baker, 1999). Overall, the level of sequence conservation at these functionally preserved lncRNA promoters is similar to that observed at protein-coding gene promoters (Figure 6F).
evidence: PhastCons analysis shown in Figure 6F compares sequence conservation between lncRNA and mRNA promoters.

claim: The developmental expression specificity of conserved lncRNA promoters is more constrained than that of many protein-coding gene promoters.
source: Their developmental expression specificity is also more constrained than that of many protein-coding gene promoters (Figure 6G).
evidence: Expression profile conservation analysis shown in Figure 6G demonstrates high constraint on lncRNA expression patterns.

claim: 195 lncRNA TSCs are specific to the melanogaster subgroup and display sequence conservation similar to protein-coding gene promoters within the subgroup.
source: To address this question, we focused on 195 lncRNA TSCs that are specific to the melanogaster subgroup, despite the orthologous sequences being present in the genomes of the two outgroups (Figure 6H). Surprisingly, they display the same degree of sequence conservation as the protein-coding gene promoters that are shared throughout the subgroup (Figure 6H).
evidence: Analysis of lineage-specific lncRNAs shown in Figure 6H demonstrates conservation within the subgroup.

claim: The selective constraints on lineage-specific lncRNAs are indeed lineage-specific as confirmed by analysis of orthologous sequences in outgroup species.
source: The assessment of conservation at orthologous sequences in outgroup species confirms that the selective constraints are indeed lineage-specific (Figure 6—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Conservation analysis in outgroups shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 6 confirms lineage-specificity.

claim: The FBgn0264479 lncRNA is 0.5 kb in length and is extremely unlikely to encode functional peptides.
source: The 0.5 kb FBgn0264479 RNA is extremely unlikely to encode functional peptides, as assessed by phyloCSF analysis (score of −217.3) and manual curation (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: PhyloCSF analysis and manual curation shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 demonstrate lack of coding potential.

claim: FBgn0264479 is highly expressed in all five species in a strikingly conserved temporal pattern restricted to a ~3 hr period encompassing the onset of gastrulation.
source: It is highly expressed in all five species surveyed, in a strikingly conserved temporal pattern restricted to a ~3 hr period encompassing the onset of gastrulation (Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Expression profiles shown in Figure 7B demonstrate conserved temporal expression pattern.

claim: Northern-blot analysis confirmed the size and expression dynamics of the FBgn0264479 transcript.
source: Northern-blot analysis confirmed the size and expression dynamics of the transcript (Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Northern blot data shown in Figure 7C validates transcript size and expression timing.

claim: The body of the FBgn0264479 transcription unit displays hallmarks of robust purifying selection within the melanogaster subgroup.
source: The body of the transcription unit displays hallmarks of robust purifying selection within the melanogaster subgroup (Figure 7A).
evidence: Sequence conservation analysis shown in Figure 7A demonstrates purifying selection.

claim: Publicly available chromatin immunoprecipitation data reveals the binding of several transcription factors to the FBgn0264479 promoter region.
source: In addition, publicly available chromatin immunoprecipitation data (Li et al., 2008; MacArthur et al., 2009) reveals the binding of several transcription factors to the promoter region (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), and their putative binding sites identified by sequence motif search also show evidence of purifying selection (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: ChIP-chip data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 demonstrates TF binding.

claim: FBgn0264479 is expressed along the ventral and dorsal midlines at the late blastoderm stage, with exclusion of lateral regions, primordial germ cells and prospective head.
source: Fluorescent in situ hybridization (FISH) in early embryos revealed expression along the ventral and dorsal midlines at the late blastoderm stage, with the exclusion of lateral regions, the primordial germ cells and the prospective head (Figure 7D).
evidence: RNA-FISH data shown in Figure 7D demonstrates spatial expression pattern.

claim: The FBgn0264479 RNA is found almost exclusively in the cytoplasm at the apical pole of cells in the late blastoderm.
source: In the late blastoderm, the RNA is found almost exclusively in the cytoplasm at the apical pole of the cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: RNA-FISH confocal imaging shown in Figure 7D demonstrates subcellular localization.

claim: The FBgn0264479 transcript is likely to be highly structured as shown by secondary structure predictions.
source: Secondary structure predictions show that the FBgn0264479 transcript is likely to be highly structured (Figure 7F), suggesting a high potential for RNA-protein interactions.
evidence: Mfold secondary structure prediction shown in Figure 7F suggests structural complexity.

claim: Core promoters define broad windows of opportunity for expression by defining a range of transcription factors from which they can receive regulatory inputs.
source: We propose a hierarchical regulatory model in which core promoters define broad windows of opportunity for expression, by defining a range of transcription factors from which they can receive regulatory inputs.
evidence: This is the proposed model based on the integration of multiple lines of evidence from the study.

claim: Core promoters may restrict regulatory inputs by recruiting different sets of general transcription factors that functionally interact with distinct groups of transcription factors.
source: Core promoters may restrict regulatory inputs by recruiting different sets of general transcription factors (GTFs) that functionally interact with distinct groups of transcription factors (Goodrich and Tjian, 2010).
evidence: This mechanistic hypothesis is proposed based on the data and supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The sequence and expression specificity of noncoding RNA promoters are evolutionarily conserved, implying biological relevance.
source: The sequence and expression specificity of noncoding RNA promoters are evolutionarily conserved, implying biological relevance.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the conservation analyses presented in the results.

claim: Noncoding transcription is extremely prevalent, tightly regulated and deeply conserved in animal development.
source: Overall, this work introduces a hierarchical model for developmental gene regulation, and reveals a major role for noncoding transcription in animal development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the comprehensive analysis of lncRNA promoters.

claim: RAMPAGE offers unprecedented specificity and detection sensitivity for TSSs.
source: It offers unprecedented specificity and detection sensitivity for TSSs, and its multiplexing capabilities allow for the seamless acquisition of high-resolution developmental time series (Batut et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a characterization of the RAMPAGE method supported by citation.

claim: Eukaryotic promoters often allow productive transcription initiation from multiple positions.
source: Since eukaryotic promoters often allow productive transcription initiation from multiple positions (Batut et al., 2013; Carninci et al., 2006; Valen et al., 2009; Hoskins et al., 2011), we use a dedicated peak-calling algorithm to group neighboring TSSs into TSS clusters (TSCs) corresponding to individual promoters (Batut et al., 2013; Batut and Gingeras, 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by multiple citations.

claim: The narrow distribution of raw RAMPAGE signal over annotated loci confirms very high specificity for true TSSs.
source: The narrow distribution of raw RAMPAGE signal (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) and of TSCs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2) over annotated loci confirms our very high specificity for true TSSs.
evidence: Metagene profile analysis shown in Figure 1C demonstrates specificity.

claim: Paired-end sequencing of cDNAs allows for evidence-based assignment of novel TSCs to existing gene annotations.
source: Importantly, paired-end sequencing of cDNAs allows for evidence-based assignment of novel TSCs to existing gene annotations, and provides valuable information about overall transcript structure (Figure 1B).
evidence: The methodology and its utility are demonstrated in Figure 1B.

claim: The variation in expression profiles across species vastly exceeds the variation across biological replicates.
source: Note that the variation across species vastly exceeds the variation across replicates, at all expression thresholds considered.
evidence: This observation is noted in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 caption.

claim: The alignments consist primarily of largely linear transformations throughout the entire series rather than local distortions.
source: Note that the alignments consist primarily of largely linear transformations (expansion/compression) throughout the entire series, rather than local distortions.
evidence: This observation is noted in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 caption describing alignment paths.

claim: The hunchback gene displays considerable conservation in the expression of both of its promoters with Pearson R2 of 0.88 and 0.97.
source: hunchback, for instance, displays considerable conservation in the expression of both of its promoters (Pearson R2 of 0.88 and 0.97), whereas the RpL19 promoter shows rapid divergence (R2 = 0.08) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Specific examples of conservation patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: The RpL19 promoter shows rapid divergence with R2 = 0.08.
source: hunchback, for instance, displays considerable conservation in the expression of both of its promoters (Pearson R2 of 0.88 and 0.97), whereas the RpL19 promoter shows rapid divergence (R2 = 0.08) (Figure 2—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Specific examples of conservation patterns shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4.

claim: Expression clusters with vastly different specificities share the same promoter structure trends.
source: Notably, expression clusters with vastly different specificities (e.g., D1 and D2) share the same promoter structure trends.
evidence: This observation is made from the analysis of core promoter motif enrichment patterns.

claim: Some TFBSs are strongly associated with specific sets of core promoter motifs.
source: The analysis of favored pairings between individual TFBSs and core promoter motifs suggests a possible synergy in the specification of expression patterns. Indeed, some TFBSs appear to be strongly associated with specific sets of core promoter motifs (Figure 3G).
evidence: Co-occurrence analysis shown in Figure 3G demonstrates associations between TFBSs and core motifs.

claim: Binding sites for the mesodermal factors srp and twi have a robust association with DRE and Ohler-7 core motifs.
source: Binding sites for the mesodermal factors srp and twi, for instance, which often tend to be found together (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), have a robust association with DRE and Ohler-7 core motifs.
evidence: Specific example of TFBS-core motif association from the analysis.

claim: Core motifs may tune the ability of a promoter to respond to specific sets of transcription factors by recruiting different sets of general transcription factors.
source: These strong affinities suggest that core motifs may tune the ability of a promoter to respond to specific sets of transcription factors. They may do so by recruiting different sets of general transcription factors (GTFs) that functionally interact with distinct groups of activators.
evidence: This mechanistic hypothesis is proposed based on the observed associations.

claim: The main areas of differential sequence conservation overlap regions preferentially occupied by precisely positioned core promoter elements and transcription factor binding sites.
source: The main areas of differential sequence conservation overlap regions preferentially occupied by precisely positioned core promoter elements (TATA, INR, DPE) and transcription factor binding sites (Figure 4A).
evidence: Conservation profile analysis shown in Figure 4A demonstrates overlap with functional elements.

claim: The correlation between expression profile and promoter sequence conservation does not hold for sequences >50 bp downstream of the TSS.
source: Importantly, this correlation does not hold for sequences >50 bp downstream of the TSS, which are likely subject to additional selective pressures on 5'-UTR and protein-coding sequences.
evidence: This observation is made from the correlation analysis and suggests different selective pressures on different regions.

claim: Ab initio motif discovery within regions of differential sequence conservation returned the canonical consensus sequences for TATA, INR and DPE.
source: Ab initio motif discovery within the regions of differential sequence conservation returned the canonical consensus sequences for TATA, INR and DPE (Figure 4E).
evidence: MEME analysis results shown in Figure 4E identify known core promoter motifs.

claim: Upstream flanking sequences tend to show higher conservation of individual TFBSs.
source: Upstream flanking sequences also tend to show higher conservation of individual TFBSs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: TFBS conservation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is possible to detect correlation between TFBS sequence conservation and expression profile conservation for some individual transcription factors.
source: Importantly, it is possible to detect such a correlation for the binding sites of some individual transcription factors (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Individual TF analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1 demonstrates factor-specific patterns.

claim: The conservation of promoter TFBS composition correlates with interspecific divergence.
source: Finally, the conservation of promoter TFBS composition, as expected, also correlates with interspecific divergence (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: TFBS composition analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Selective constraints on developmental expression timing act particularly strongly on core promoter elements, most notably Initiator, DPE and TATA elements.
source: These observations establish a clear relationship between core promoter sequence and expression specificity. Selective constraints on developmental expression timing act particularly strongly on core promoter elements, most notably Initiator, DPE and TATA elements.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the conservation analyses of core promoter elements.

claim: The true TSC conservation rate is expected to be within the 49-75% range.
source: As some peaks lack alignments owing to genuine insertions or deletions, we expect the true conservation rate to be within the 49–75% range.
evidence: This range is inferred from the analysis of all TSCs versus those with syntenic alignments.

claim: TSCs with lower expression levels tend to be less conserved, but general trends are shared between TSCs of all expression levels.
source: Although TSCs with lower expression levels tend to be less conserved, general trends are shared between TSCs of all expression levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Expression level-stratified conservation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Overall, promoters evolve no more slowly, and possibly even faster, than TFBSs.
source: Comparison to published data on the evolution of Twist binding sites (He et al., 2011) revealed that overall, promoters evolve no more slowly, and possibly even faster, than TFBSs do (Figure 5—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Comparison with published TFBS evolution data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 4.

claim: A very substantial proportion of non-genic promoters is deeply conserved (active in all five species analyzed).
source: There is, however, a very substantial proportion of non-genic promoters that is deeply conserved (i.e., active in all five species analyzed), suggesting the possibility of widespread functionality.
evidence: This observation is made from the conservation analysis of non-genic promoters.

claim: The detection of lncRNA TSCs is highly reproducible across D. melanogaster biological replicates.
source: The detection of lncRNA TSCs is highly reproducible across D. melanogaster biological replicates (Figure 6E).
evidence: Replicate analysis shown in Figure 6E demonstrates reproducibility.

claim: Of all D. melanogaster lncRNA TSCs, 2016 can be aligned to the D. pseudoobscura genome assembly and 1111 are functionally conserved.
source: Of all D. melanogaster lncRNA TSCs, 2016 can be aligned to the D. pseudoobscura genome assembly and 1111 are functionally conserved (Figure 6E), suggesting that they have been maintained since the last common ancestor of these two species.
evidence: Conservation analysis shown in Figure 6E quantifies lncRNA promoter conservation.

claim: The conserved lncRNA promoter set includes well-known essential noncoding transcription units such as bithoraxoid and roX1.
source: This set includes well-known essential noncoding transcription units, such as bithoraxoid (Lipshitz et al., 1987; Petruk et al., 2006) (Figure 6—figure supplement 4) and roX1 (Franke and Baker, 1999).
evidence: Specific examples of known functional lncRNAs included in the conserved set.

claim: 1529 lncRNA promoters are shared between the 3 species of the melanogaster subgroup and display high sequence conservation within the subgroup.
source: Therefore, to place a more reasonable lower bound on the true number of conserved lncRNA promoters, we focused on those shared between the 3 species of the melanogaster subgroup. These 1529 promoters similarly display a high degree of sequence conservation within the subgroup, and their expression specificity also appears constrained (Figure 6—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Subgroup-specific conservation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Lineage-specific lncRNAs have come under purifying selection after acquiring lineage-specific functions.
source: This argues that these evolutionarily recent lncRNAs have come under purifying selection after acquiring lineage-specific functions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation of conservation within the lineage but not in outgroups.

claim: A substantial proportion of lncRNAs may be under purifying selection for biological functions relevant to embryonic development.
source: Taken together, our observations raise the possibility that a substantial proportion of lncRNAs may indeed be under purifying selection for biological functions relevant to embryonic development.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple lines of evidence for lncRNA conservation.

claim: FBgn0264479 has been annotated based on EST data but has never been characterized.
source: This is an intriguing embryonic transcript that, although it has been annotated based on expressed sequence tag (EST) data, has to our knowledge never been characterized.
evidence: This statement describes the prior knowledge status of the locus.

claim: The FBgn0264479 early expression domain evolves into a complex segmented pattern by the end of germband extension.
source: This early expression domain subsequently evolves into a complex segmented pattern by the end of germband extension (Figure 7D).
evidence: RNA-FISH time series shown in Figure 7D demonstrates temporal evolution of expression pattern.

claim: The FBgn0264479 RNA appears to be generally concentrated in a single major focus per cell at the late blastoderm stage.
source: It appears at that stage to be generally concentrated in a single major focus per cell (Figure 7E).
evidence: High-resolution RNA-FISH imaging shown in Figure 7E demonstrates punctate localization.

claim: The putative binding sites for transcription factors at the FBgn0264479 promoter show evidence of purifying selection.
source: In addition, publicly available chromatin immunoprecipitation data (Li et al., 2008; MacArthur et al., 2009) reveals the binding of several transcription factors to the promoter region (Figure 7—figure supplement 2), and their putative binding sites identified by sequence motif search also show evidence of purifying selection (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: TFBS conservation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 demonstrates selection on binding sites.

claim: The expression dynamics of transcription factors are consistent with their regulating the FBgn0264479 promoter.
source: The expression dynamics of the transcription factors are consistent with their regulating the FBgn0264479 promoter (Figure 7—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Expression profile comparison shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 4 demonstrates temporal compatibility.

claim: The FBgn0264479 lncRNA is expressed in a spatial profile highly similar to that of the schnurri gene.
source: Interestingly, this lncRNA is expressed in a spatial profile highly similar to that of the schnurri gene (Arora et al., 1995), which is part of the Dpp (TGF-β/Smad) signaling pathway and plays an essential role in the establishment of dorsoventral embryo polarity (Arora et al., 1995; Dai et al., 2000).
evidence: Comparison with known gene expression patterns supported by citations.

claim: The punctate cytoplasmic localization pattern of FBgn0264479 is reminiscent of the targeting of multiple Dpp pathway components to endosomes in larval wing discs.
source: The punctate cytoplasmic localization pattern of the FBgn0264479 lncRNA is reminiscent of the targeting of multiple Dpp pathway components to endosomes in larval wing discs (Bökel et al., 2006; Coumailleau et al., 2009; González-Gaitán, 2003).
evidence: Comparison with known subcellular localization patterns supported by citations.

claim: Endosomes localize apically in the late embryonic blastoderm.
source: Endosomes localize apically in the late embryonic blastoderm (Fabrowski et al., 2013), and mutants for Sara, the Smad endosome-targeting factor (Bökel et al., 2006; González-Gaitán, 2003), die early in embryogenesis (Bökel et al., 2006), suggesting that endosome-based signaling is also essential at that stage.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: There is an intriguing possibility of a role for the FBgn0264479 lncRNA in TGF-β signaling.
source: This raises the intriguing possibility of a role for the FBgn0264479 lncRNA in TGF-β signaling, a crucial pathway in all animals that plays a major role in human disease, including cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the expression pattern and localization similarities.

claim: LncRNAs have been shown to regulate transcription and chromatin structure, as well as mRNA stability and protein localization.
source: In recent years, it has become clear that noncoding transcription serves a myriad of molecular functions in Eukaryotes, and plays a part in virtually every known biological process (Augui et al., 2011; Ulitsky and Bartel, 2013; Guttman and Rinn, 2012; Ponting et al., 2009). LncRNAs have been shown to regulate transcription and chromatin structure, as well as mRNA stability and protein localization.
evidence: This is established knowledge from the cited literature.

claim: Sometimes it is the transcription of the locus itself that plays a mechanistic role, rather than the resulting transcript.
source: Sometimes it is the transcription of the locus itself that plays a mechanistic role, rather than the resulting transcript – as in the case of the upstream bxd promoter (Petruk et al., 2006), which has one of the most highly conserved expression profiles that we have observed.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature with supporting observation from the current data.

claim: D. melanogaster is an excellent model for exploring the diverse functions of lncRNAs with targeted genetic and molecular studies.
source: Our work provides evolutionary evidence for a broad biological relevance of noncoding transcription to developmental processes, and establishes D. melanogaster as an excellent model for exploring the diverse functions of lncRNAs with targeted genetic and molecular studies.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comprehensive characterization of lncRNAs in Drosophila.

claim: Core promoters are generally not thought to play a significant regulatory role.
source: Core promoters, generally not thought to play a significant regulatory role, in fact impart restrictions on the developmental timing of gene expression on a global scale.
evidence: This statement describes the prevailing view that the study challenges.

claim: Enhancers are generally thought to be the primary determinants of gene expression specificity.
source: Sequences that bind transcriptional activators and repressors, known as enhancers (Banerji et al., 1981; Banerji et al., 1983; Zinn et al., 1983; Small et al., 1991; Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Schaffner, 2015; Benoist and Chambon, 1980), are generally thought to be the primary determinants of gene expression specificity.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Core promoters are usually assumed to be structural elements that contribute little or no regulatory information.
source: Sequences that serve as docking sites for the basal transcription machinery, the core promoters (Lenhard et al., 2012), are usually assumed to be structural elements that contribute little or no regulatory information.
evidence: This statement describes the prevailing assumption that the study challenges.

claim: Core promoters contain sequence motifs that serve as a platform for RNA Pol II initiation at transcription start sites but are not by themselves sufficient to induce transcription.
source: Indeed, core promoters contain sequence motifs (e.g., TATA boxes) that serve as a platform for RNA Pol II initiation at transcription start sites (TSSs), but are not by themselves sufficient to induce transcription (Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Lenhard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Interacting core promoter-enhancer pairs may be directly adjacent or located hundreds of kilobases apart in metazoan genomes.
source: Interacting core promoter-enhancer pairs may be directly adjacent (Zinn et al., 1983; Benoist and Chambon, 1980; Zabidi et al., 2015), or may be located hundreds of kilobases apart in metazoan genomes (Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Lettice et al., 2003), and the rules enforcing specific interactions are unknown (Spitz and Furlong, 2012; Lenhard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: There is evidence that core promoters can influence the expression specificity of some genes.
source: There is evidence that core promoters can influence the expression specificity of some genes (Zabidi et al., 2015; Goodrich and Tjian, 2010; Haberle et al., 2014), but so far this has not been systematically studied in the context of development.
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature that motivates the current study.

claim: Noncoding transcription is very prevalent in Eukaryotes.
source: Indeed, it has become increasingly clear that noncoding transcription is very prevalent in Eukaryotes (Kapranov et al., 2007; Djebali et al., 2012; Graveley et al., 2011; Gerstein et al., 2010; Young et al., 2012; Derrien et al., 2012)
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: Both genetic and biochemical studies have unambiguously established long noncoding RNAs as functional components of the cellular machinery.
source: and both genetic and biochemical studies have unambiguously established long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) as functional components of the cellular machinery (Augui et al., 2011; Ulitsky and Bartel, 2013; Guttman and Rinn, 2012; Ponting et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: The use of genome-wide functional assays in a phylogenetic framework is a powerful and general approach to deciphering regulatory sequences and assessing biological relevance of lncRNAs.
source: Deciphering the meaning of regulatory sequences, or assessing the biological relevance of lncRNA genes, are daunting tasks that require innovative strategies. The use of genome-wide functional assays in a phylogenetic framework is a powerful and general approach to such questions (Tsankov et al., 2011; Schmidt et al., 2010; Stefflova et al., 2013; He et al., 2011).
evidence: This methodological approach is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Direct measurements of complex genome functions in multiple species provide a genomic Rosetta Stone from which the underlying code can begin to be parsed out.
source: Indeed, direct measurements of complex genome functions in multiple species provide a sort of genomic Rosetta Stone from which the underlying code can begin to be parsed out.
evidence: This is a conceptual framework for the comparative genomics approach.

claim: The study successfully detected in vivo some functional associations between Dref and housekeeping promoters, and between Trl and some developmentally regulated promoters, that were recently described in vitro.
source: Of note, we successfully detected in vivo some functional associations between Dref and housekeeping promoters, and between Trl and some developmentally regulated promoters, that were recently described in vitro (Zabidi et al., 2015) (Figure 3).
evidence: This validates previous in vitro findings with in vivo data from the current study.

claim: The study generalizes the concept of specific interactions between core promoters and enhancer sequences and demonstrates its global relevance in a developmental context.
source: Our analysis generalizes the concept of specific interactions between core promoters and enhancer sequences, and demonstrates for the first time its global relevance in a developmental context.
evidence: This is a key conclusion of the study based on the comprehensive analysis.

claim: In a hierarchical model of transcriptional control, core promoters and enhancers mediate coarse-grained and fine-grained developmental regulation, respectively.
source: We propose a two-tier model of transcriptional control in which core promoters and enhancers mediate, respectively, coarse-grained and fine-grained developmental regulation.
evidence: This is the proposed hierarchical model based on the study's findings.

claim: Some GTFs have been shown to shape the expression specificity of individual promoters.
source: Some GTFs have been shown to shape the expression specificity of individual promoters, and it is known that different activators and repressors have distinct requirements for cofactors and GTFs (Zabidi et al., 2015; Goodrich and Tjian, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge from cited literature.

claim: What applies to time may also apply to space in terms of core promoter/enhancer interplay specifying gene expression.
source: Notably, what applies to time may also apply to space, and it is possible that similar core promoter/enhancer interplay hierarchically specifies gene expression in broad developmental lineages and individual cell types.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the temporal findings to spatial regulation.

claim: The study previously reported the existence of 7421 putative lncRNA promoters in an analysis of the whole D. melanogaster life cycle.
source: Our findings likely apply to other developmental stages as well, as we previously reported the existence of 7421 putative lncRNA promoters in an analysis of the whole D. melanogaster life cycle (Batut et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: The study detected the expression of only 205 of 1119 recently identified lncRNAs.
source: In addition, we detected the expression of only 205 of 1119 recently identified lncRNAs (Young et al., 2012).
evidence: Comparison with previously published lncRNA catalog.

claim: The study is only beginning to scratch the surface of lncRNA biology in Drosophila.
source: This suggests that we are only beginning to scratch the surface of lncRNA biology in Drosophila.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the comparison with other lncRNA studies.

claim: A melanogaster subgroup core set of at least 1529 lncRNA promoters is under substantial selective constraint.
source: A melanogaster subgroup core set of at least 1529 is under substantial selective constraint, and most of those are therefore highly likely to have biologically relevant activities.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the conservation analysis within the melanogaster subgroup.

claim: lncRNA genes evolve faster than their protein-coding counterparts in agreement with previous reports.
source: In agreement with previous reports (Derrien et al., 2012; Haerty and Ponting, 2013; Kutter et al., 2012), we find that lncRNA genes evolve faster than their protein-coding counterparts.
evidence: This observation is consistent with cited previous studies.

claim: The observation that lineage-specific lncRNAs are under substantial selective pressure reveals that noncoding transcription may be a major driver of phenotypic diversification and organismal adaptation.
source: Our observation that lineage-specific lncRNAs are also under substantial selective pressure reveals that noncoding transcription may be a major driver of phenotypic diversification and organismal adaptation.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the analysis of lineage-specific lncRNA conservation.

claim: Transposable elements play an important role in the evolutionary gain of promoters, particularly lncRNA promoters.
source: We recently showed that transposable elements play an important role in the evolutionary gain of promoters, and in particular of lncRNA promoters (Batut et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a reference to previous work by the authors.

claim: Transposon proliferation is a major mechanism favoring the neofunctionalization of intergenic regions as sources of biologically active noncoding transcripts.
source: We propose that transposon proliferation is a major mechanism favoring the neofunctionalization of intergenic regions as sources of biologically active noncoding transcripts.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on previous findings and current observations.

claim: The FBgn0264479 lncRNA has been under strong purifying selection over at least 25-50 million years.
source: Although further characterization will be required to decipher the precise biological role of this transcript, our observations definitively establish its developmental expression specificity, clearly point to a non-protein-coding function, and show that it has been under strong purifying selection over at least 25–50 million years.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the conservation analysis and functional characterization of FBgn0264479.

claim: Systematic efforts on a larger scale will illuminate the biology of lncRNAs.
source: We expect that systematic efforts on a larger scale will illuminate the biology of a long-ignored class of genes that has proven its worth.
evidence: This is a forward-looking statement about future research directions.

claim: Total RNA was extracted from embryos using a Beadbeater with zirconia beads and the RNAdvance Tissue kit.
source: Total RNA was extracted from embryos using a Beadbeater (Biospec, Cat. #607) with 1.0 mm zirconia beads (Biospec, #11079110zx) and the RNAdvance Tissue kit (Agencourt #A32649) according to the manufacturer's instructions, including DNaseI treatment.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: 5'-monophosphate transcripts were depleted by TEX digest.
source: 5'-monophosphate transcripts were depleted by TEX digest (Epicentre #TER51020).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Each library was sequenced on one lane of an Illumina HiSeq 2000.
source: Each library was sequenced on one lane of an Illumina HiSeq 2000.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Reads were mapped to the appropriate reference genomes using the STAR aligner.
source: Reads were mapped to the appropriate reference genomes using the STAR aligner (Dobin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: A peak was considered absent in a target species if it had at least a 100-fold lower signal than in the reference species.
source: A peak was considered absent in a target species if it had at least a 100-fold lower signal than in the reference species.
evidence: This is a methodological criterion for determining functional conservation.

claim: The phylogenetic tree was inferred by treating the presence/absence of each peak as a 2-state discrete character using the MIX and PARS programs of the PHYLIP suite.
source: The phylogenetic tree was inferred by treating the presence/absence of each peak as a 2-state discrete character, sequentially using the MIX and PARS program of the PHYLIP suite according to the recommendations of the software documentation (http://evolution.genetics.washington.edu/phylip.html).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the phylogenetic reconstruction approach.

claim: Per-base conservation scores were computed by running the phastCons and phyloP programs of the PHAST suite v1.1 on the MultiZ alignment.
source: Per-base conservation scores were computed by running the phastCons and phyloP programs of the PHAST suite v1.1 on the MultiZ alignment according to the recommendations of the software documentation (http://compgen.bscb.cornell.edu/phast).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the sequence conservation analysis.
